content: Cor pulmonale refers to the failure of the right side of the heart, which occurs due to prolonged high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries and the right ventricle of the heart. Symptoms of Cor Pulmonale: Patients may experience chest discomfort, typically localized to the anterior chest. There is often a reduced tolerance for physical activity or exercise. Shortness of breath is a common symptom. Swelling in the feet or ankles may occur. Symptoms related to underlying conditions, such as wheezing or coughing, may also be present. Causes of Cor Pulmonale: Normally, the left side of the heart generates higher blood pressure to pump blood throughout the body, while the right side pumps blood through the lungs at a much lower pressure. Any condition that results in sustained high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries (pulmonary hypertension) places stress on the right side of the heart. When the right ventricle cannot effectively pump against these abnormally high pressures, the condition is termed cor pulmonale. Chronic lung diseases or conditions that cause prolonged low blood oxygen levels can lead to cor pulmonale. Examples include: Central sleep apnea Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease Cystic fibrosis Interstitial lung disease Kyphoscoliosis Obstructive sleep apnea Pneumoconiosis Primary pulmonary hypertension Pulmonary vascular disease Secondary pulmonary hypertension When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Immediate medical attention is necessary if you experience shortness of breath or chest pain. Diagnosis: Physical examination findings may include: Abnormal fluid accumulation in the abdomen (ascites) Abnormal heart sounds Bluish discoloration of the skin (cyanosis) Enlargement of the liver Swelling of the neck veins, indicating elevated right-heart pressures Swelling of the ankles Diagnostic tests that may assist in confirming cor pulmonale include: Blood antibody tests Blood tests for brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) Chest X-ray CT scan of the chest Echocardiogram Lung biopsy (rarely performed) Measurement of blood oxygen levels via arterial blood gas (ABG) Pulmonary function tests Right heart catheterization Ventilation and perfusion (V/Q) scan of the lungs Treatment Options: Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying condition causing cor pulmonale. Supplemental oxygen may be prescribed to increase blood oxygen levels. Medications commonly used include: Bosentan or sildenafil, administered orally Calcium channel blockers, often used in early cases Prostacyclin, which can be delivered via injection or inhalation Anticoagulant medications (blood thinners) may also be prescribed. Surgical intervention may be required to correct heart defects contributing to the condition. In advanced cases, a heart and lung transplant may be considered. Prognosis: The outcome depends on the underlying cause of the condition. Oxygen therapy often improves symptoms, physical stamina, and survival rates. Treating primary pulmonary hypertension can lead to improved stamina and longer life expectancy. In some cases, lung transplantation or heart-lung transplantation can extend survival. Possible Complications: Progressive pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale can result in: Life-threatening shortness of breath Severe fluid retention Shock Death Prevention: Avoiding behaviors that contribute to chronic lung disease, such as cigarette smoking, may prevent the development of cor pulmonale. Careful evaluation of childhood heart murmurs may help prevent cor pulmonale caused by certain congenital heart defects.
